notes: 9.1.4 from 14 drivers in one bar, with four height channels and Sonos' Sound Motion woofer doing the bass instead of a separate box. Everything it can be expanded with - Sub 4, Sub Mini, two Era 300 rears - is wireless, so nothing in the system is ever cabled. One eARC socket and no HDMI input, so it cannot sit between a console and the TV.

Nine drivers including two that fire upward as dipoles for the height channels, with Bose's TrueSpace upmixing everything else. The Bass Module 500/700 and the wireless surround speakers are optional and wireless. Reviewers put its height effects below the Sonos Arc Ultra's; it is the smaller box of the two.

5.1.2 in one bar with two height channels, Dolby Atmos and DTS:X, eARC plus one 4K passthrough HDMI input, and RCA inputs for a turntable. The Heston Sub 200 is the matching wireless subwoofer and is sold separately; reviews praise the bass it manages without one. Driver and power counts differ between reviews (9 or 11 drivers, 150 W or 320 W), so those figures are not recorded here.

5.1.2 from eleven drivers: six racetrack mid-woofers, three tweeters and two 2.75-inch up-firing units, rated 315 W RMS, with Dolby Atmos and DTS:X. The Enchant wireless subwoofer and wireless surrounds expand it. One comparison table prints 9.0.2 instead of 5.1.2; the manufacturer's own page and Which?'s review agree on 5.1.2.

3.1.2 with real up-firing height drivers, which is what separates it from the Flexus Core 100 on the rejected list. It takes up to two wireless Flexus subwoofers and wireless Flexus surrounds, so the system stays cable-free as it grows. What Hi-Fi calls its Atmos convincing for the money.

Electroline and Stephanis both print 3.1.2 with a wireless subwoofer, which would make this the cheapest true-Atmos system on the list by a wide margin. Both the layout and the up-firing drivers come from the retailer listings only, so treat the entry as unconfirmed until you check JBL's own page - the Cinema line is where JBL puts its virtual-Atmos bars.
